title: Leading by example and recognising the crew
moduleTitle: Shared: Growing and managing a team
audience: Team leaders who want to set the standard through their own conduct and build a steady, fair work culture on the crew.
learningOutcomes: Identify three behaviours a lead must model to get the crew's standard.
Apply rules consistently to every crew member, including the lead.
Plan a recognition practice that fits the business's budget and values.

instruction.heading: Leading by example
instruction.body: A crew copies what the lead does, not what the lead says. If the lead cuts corners, the crew learns that corners can be cut. Show the attitude and behaviour you want: arrive on time, follow the checklist, clean up after yourself and speak respectfully to the client and the crew. A lead who takes part in the work, rather than standing back, earns more trust when the crew needs help on a hard job.

instruction.heading: Consistent rules and fair treatment
instruction.body: Crew members need confidence that rules bind everyone equally. Apply the same standards to the lead, to new workers and to long-standing staff. When an exception is needed, explain it openly so nobody assumes favouritism. Balance matters too: a crew that works on weekends or late shifts should also get breaks and time to rest, and the lead should watch for signs of overload.

instruction.heading: Recognition that costs little
instruction.body: Acknowledgement is among the most useful instruments a lead can use. It does not need to be expensive. A short message after a good week, a shout-out at the shift briefing, or a shared lunch after a hard job all work. Name what was done well and why it mattered to the client or the crew. Tie recognition to the values the business has stated, so that the crew sees a clear link between behaviour and the standard.

procedure: Write down three behaviours you want the crew to show, and check that you show each one yourself on your shifts.
Write down the crew rules and check that each one applies to the lead as well.
Notice one exception you have made recently and decide whether to explain it to the crew.
Plan one low-cost recognition practice for the next two weeks and name the behaviour it rewards.
Link the recognition to one stated business value.
Review the crew's response after two weeks and adjust the practice.

workedExamples.situation: A commercial crew lead starts to leave the final walk-through to the crew and finishes early. The crew begins doing the same, and walk-throughs are missed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What should the lead change, and how should the crew be told?
workedExamples.reasoning: The lead returns to the walk-through, explains why it matters to the client, and asks the crew what made it hard to fit in. A short recognition message the following week names the crew members who completed it, which reinforces the behaviour.

equipmentAndPpe: No specialist equipment. Standard PPE and the crew's checklist.

commonErrors.error: Asking the crew to follow rules the lead does not follow.
commonErrors.prevention: Check your own conduct against each rule before you brief the crew.

commonErrors.error: Recognition that is generic and never linked to the work.
commonErrors.prevention: Name the specific action and the result it produced.
Explain the reason for any exception at the next briefing.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Rest breaks, shift length and overtime rules depend on the employment arrangements and are not set by this lesson.

qualityStandard: The learner lists three modelled behaviours and can show an example of each from the job.
The recognition plan names a specific behaviour, a method and a date to review it.
documentationEvidence: Written list of crew rules showing that they apply to the lead.
Recognition log with the behaviour, the method and the date.
summary: A crew copies the lead's conduct, so the lead models the standard.
Apply rules to everyone and explain any exception.
Recognition works best when it is specific, timely and tied to a stated value.

knowledgeChecks.question: What does a crew most often copy from its lead?
options: The lead's conduct on the job
The lead's rank in the business

knowledgeChecks.question: A lead gives one worker a shorter checklist without explanation. What is the main problem?
options: The worker will finish faster and the job will be quicker for the client
The crew may assume favouritism because the rule was not applied the same way
The checklist is too long and the worker has complained about it for a while
The client will not notice and the lead will be praised for it by the team

knowledgeChecks.question: Which recognition approach best matches this lesson?
options: Wait for an annual event and give the thanks in a card at the end of the year
Give a generic thank you to the whole business at the end of the year
Name the specific action and its result in a short message soon after it happened
Only recognise the lead's own work and ignore the crew entirely in the report
